Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Data Provenance Initiative

Data Provenance Initiative is a volunteer collective of AI researchers auditing AI training data: 1,800+ text datasets in its 2023 first release, now four public measurement systems from datasets and web consent to model markets and real use (its pages); the archive sets it in the licensing dimension of provenance, bounded at the corpus (#725).

🗂️ What it is

  • Operator: a "volunteer effort"; paper by Longpre and 16 others (README; arXiv; census); MIT researchers among its founders (MIT Sloan).3↘
    The Data Provenance Initiative is, in its repository's words, "a multi-disciplinary volunteer effort to improve transparency, documentation, and responsible use of training datasets for AI," and on its About page "a volunteer collective of AI researchers conducting large-scale audits of the systems and resources that shape modern AI" (README; dataprovenance.org/about); the provenance census record gives its operator as the Initiative itself, a "volunteer effort" with a "paper by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors," kinds it an "audit collection and explorer" and sets it in the lineage of "training data" (provenance census record).§1 MIT Sloan's account has "a team of multidisciplinary researchers, including professor Sandy Pentland and others from MIT," create the Initiative "to tackle the data transparency challenge head-on" (MIT Sloan, 3 March 2025), and the home page says that "DPI releases papers, datasets, and dashboards that help researchers, journalists, policymakers, and builders reason from shared evidence" (dataprovenance.org).§2 The founding paper was submitted on 25 October 2023 and revised on 4 November 2023, "by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors" (arXiv:2310.16787), and published in Nature Machine Intelligence, volume 6, on 30 August 2024 (Nature Machine Intelligence); the census dates the entity from the preprint, "2023 (arXiv:2310.16787, v1 25 October 2023)" (provenance census record).§7
  • Data provenance: a dataset's "sourcing, creation and licensing heritage" (Nature MI), traced to source, creators, licences, use (arXiv; census).2↘
    The founding audit's authors name its object: "we term the combination of these indicators, including a dataset's sourcing, creation and licensing heritage, as well as its characteristics, the 'data provenance'" (Nature Machine Intelligence, 30 August 2024), traced "from their source, creators, series of license conditions, properties, and subsequent use" (arXiv:2310.16787), and the home page's "Training Data Provenance" traces "the sources, licenses, creators, languages, geographies, and derivation chains behind public AI training datasets" (dataprovenance.org).§4 The provenance census asks of each entity it formalizes "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" and answers for the Initiative that it records, of the three capabilities express, record and test: its object "a fine-tuning dataset, traced through its collection to its sources," its unit "a dataset within a collection," its relations derivation, creators, licences and subsequent use, the last field restating the paper's lineage (provenance census record).§5
  • Its dimension: training-corpus licensing: "Under what permissions did this data enter this system?" (#725).1↘
    #725 sets that object in the second dimension of provenance, "training-corpus licensing," which "has academic instrumentation and emerging legal architecture," its object "The corpus" and its question "Under what permissions did this data enter this system?", with the Initiative among its frameworks and among provenance's disciplinary homes as "dataset documentation (DPI, model cards, dataset cards)," and states that the dimensions of artifact, licensing and meaning are independent: "a licensed dataset can produce outputs with excellent semantic provenance if the synthesis preserves attribution" (#725).§6

🧾 Origin and extent

  • Founding audit: 1800+ text datasets, 25 Oct 2023 (arXiv); 1,858 in 44 collections (Nature MI, 2024).3↘
    The founding paper was submitted on 25 October 2023 and revised on 4 November 2023, "by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors" (arXiv:2310.16787), and published in Nature Machine Intelligence, volume 6, on 30 August 2024 (Nature Machine Intelligence); the census dates the entity from the preprint, "2023 (arXiv:2310.16787, v1 25 October 2023)" (provenance census record).§7 It convened "a multi-disciplinary effort between legal and machine learning experts to systematically audit and trace 1800+ text datasets" (arXiv), in the journal "44 instruction or 'alignment' finetuning data collections composed of 1,858 individual datasets" (Nature Machine Intelligence), the release the repository calls the Data Provenance Collection and "this initiative's first release" (README), and the count the census carries, "44 data collections, 1800+ fine-tuning text-to-text datasets (first release)," as of the README (provenance census record); MIT Sloan gives "more than 1,800 text datasets" from "44 of the most widely used text data collections" (MIT Sloan).§8 The journal gives the measure by platform, "more than 70% of licences for popular datasets on GitHub and Hugging Face are 'unspecified'" and "66% of analysed Hugging Face licences were in a different use category, often labelled as more permissive than the author's original licence," and names "a crisis in licence laundering" (Nature Machine Intelligence); MIT Sloan restates error rates "greater than 50%" and omission rates "of more than 70%" (MIT Sloan).§15
  • Tools: Explorer, Collection and Card, "symbolic attribution for all constituent datasets" (README).2↘
    With the audit came "an interactive UI, the Data Provenance Explorer, which allows practitioners to trace and filter on data provenance for the most popular open source finetuning data collections" (arXiv), in the journal "an open-source repository for downloading, filtering and exploring data provenance and characteristics" whose tools "auto-generate data provenance cards for scalable symbolic attribution" (Nature Machine Intelligence); the repository's Data Provenance Card is "symbolic attribution for all constituent datasets, that can be used as structured documentation" (README), "human-readable" in MIT Sloan's account (MIT Sloan), and the census carries it as the entity's provenance carrier beside "audit metadata per dataset" (provenance census record).§9 The census gives Data Provenance Explorer, Data Provenance Collection and Data Provenance Card as other names of the entity and states its relation to them twice: among its negative tags, "initiative, explorer and collection are distinct records," and on its sibling relation to the MMRS meta-aggregator's record of the explorer, "the same entity, read for reception there and for provenance carriage here"; it records the Explorer as "a JavaScript application, unreadable to a plain fetch" (provenance census record).§10
  • Now: 4,000+ datasets audited, 14,000 web domains tracked, 851k open models, 23,158 conversations (home page).3↘
    Its work, the About page says, "began with training data provenance: tracing datasets from origin to creation, cataloging sources, licenses, creators, and documentation practices" and "now also covers web consent, open model markets, concentration of power, and how people use AI systems in practice" (dataprovenance.org/about); the home page calls it "Public measurement infrastructure for AI data, model ecosystems, and real-world AI use," which "maps the datasets, web policies, model markets, and real-world AI uses that shape how AI systems are built and governed" through "Four public measurement systems" (dataprovenance.org).§3 The home page's four systems are the Data Provenance Explorer ("4,000+ datasets," "608 languages across text, speech, and video," inspecting "dataset sources, licenses, creators, geographies, modalities, and derivation chains"), the Web Consent Explorer ("14,000 domains," "Terms, robots.txt, and crawl restrictions"), Open Model Evolution ("851k open models," "2.2B downloads") and The AI Observatory ("23,158 conversations," "85,633 turns from 7 public sources") (dataprovenance.org).§11 Its metrics read "4,000+" "datasets audited," "14,000" "web domains tracked," "851k" "open models measured" and "23,158" "AI conversations annotated," and its publications carry the later work: Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024), the multimodal audit, "An audit of four thousand public text, speech, and video datasets" (ICLR 2025), Economies of Open Intelligence (preprint) and The AI Observatory (NeurIPS 2026) (dataprovenance.org); in March 2025 MIT Sloan still had the work "currently focused on the data provenance of text," with a plan "to expand to other media, such as video" (MIT Sloan).§12
  • Later audits: Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024); four thousand text, speech and video datasets (ICLR 2025).1↘
    Its metrics read "4,000+" "datasets audited," "14,000" "web domains tracked," "851k" "open models measured" and "23,158" "AI conversations annotated," and its publications carry the later work: Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024), the multimodal audit, "An audit of four thousand public text, speech, and video datasets" (ICLR 2025), Economies of Open Intelligence (preprint) and The AI Observatory (NeurIPS 2026) (dataprovenance.org); in March 2025 MIT Sloan still had the work "currently focused on the data provenance of text," with a plan "to expand to other media, such as video" (MIT Sloan).§12
  • The record: the census keeps the first release's count, the composition "ahead of the record" (Capture Registry).1↘
    The census carries the entity as "active" and lists "the Explorer itself (JavaScript)" and "the multimodal extension (arXiv:2412.17847)" among what it has not yet checked (provenance census record); the Capture Registry finds that "The record has one explorer and the first release's count," that the home-page card gives "four platforms and '4,000+ audited datasets; 14,000 tracked web domains'," that the composition is "ahead of the record on the entity's current extent," and that "The census is to re-read dataprovenance.org and carry the platforms and the current count with their quotes," the capture being "a correction to be made from the entity's own page" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§13
  • One record or three: "distinct records", and "the same entity" as the explorer's MMRS record (census).1↘
    The census gives Data Provenance Explorer, Data Provenance Collection and Data Provenance Card as other names of the entity and states its relation to them twice: among its negative tags, "initiative, explorer and collection are distinct records," and on its sibling relation to the MMRS meta-aggregator's record of the explorer, "the same entity, read for reception there and for provenance carriage here"; it records the Explorer as "a JavaScript application, unreadable to a plain fetch" (provenance census record).§10

🔎 Findings

  • Licences: omission 70%+, errors 50%+ on hosting sites (arXiv); 66% of Hugging Face licences recategorized (Nature MI).5↘
    It convened "a multi-disciplinary effort between legal and machine learning experts to systematically audit and trace 1800+ text datasets" (arXiv), in the journal "44 instruction or 'alignment' finetuning data collections composed of 1,858 individual datasets" (Nature Machine Intelligence), the release the repository calls the Data Provenance Collection and "this initiative's first release" (README), and the count the census carries, "44 data collections, 1800+ fine-tuning text-to-text datasets (first release)," as of the README (provenance census record); MIT Sloan gives "more than 1,800 text datasets" from "44 of the most widely used text data collections" (MIT Sloan).§8 The founding audit observed "frequent miscategorization of licenses on widely used dataset hosting sites, with license omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+," which "points to a crisis in misattribution and informed use of the most popular datasets driving many recent breakthroughs" (arXiv), the result the census records as what survived the operation it tested, "dataset repackaging and hosting (licence carried or lost on hosting sites)" (provenance census record).§14 The journal gives the measure by platform, "more than 70% of licences for popular datasets on GitHub and Hugging Face are 'unspecified'" and "66% of analysed Hugging Face licences were in a different use category, often labelled as more permissive than the author's original licence," and names "a crisis in licence laundering" (Nature Machine Intelligence); MIT Sloan restates error rates "greater than 50%" and omission rates "of more than 70%" (MIT Sloan).§15 The Capture Registry checked these figures "against the provenance census record of the same day and the entity pages it saved" and calls the 70%/50% wording "the record's quote from the repository README" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), where the census gives it as what "the founding paper reports" (provenance census record).§16 "In total, 85% of dataset licences request attribution, and 30% include a share-alike clause" (Nature Machine Intelligence); #725 carries these figures with the omission and error rates and reads them as the licensing dimension's ground, "The DPI's documentation of 70%+ license-omission rates establishes the licensing dimension's urgency" (#725), and #1714 reads the finding as "how much is lost before training even begins" (#1714).§17
  • Attribution: 85% of licences request it, 30% share-alike (Nature MI; #725).1↘
    "In total, 85% of dataset licences request attribution, and 30% include a share-alike clause" (Nature Machine Intelligence); #725 carries these figures with the omission and error rates and reads them as the licensing dimension's ground, "The DPI's documentation of 70%+ license-omission rates establishes the licensing dimension's urgency" (#725), and #1714 reads the finding as "how much is lost before training even begins" (#1714).§17
  • Divide: closed datasets hold lower-resource languages and creative tasks (arXiv); non-commercial licences 61% in 2023 (Nature MI).1↘
    Of the commercial divide the preprint finds "closed datasets monopolizing important categories: lower resource languages, more creative tasks, richer topic variety, newer and more synthetic training data" (arXiv); the journal records that "In 2023 there was a spike in NC/A-O dataset licences," "the NC/A-O rate is 61%" that year, and that "a full 45% of NC/A-O datasets are synthetic, compared to <14% in more permissive licence categories" (Nature Machine Intelligence); the home page's findings are "Source content often carries stricter terms than dataset releases," "Open weights now outpace truly open-source models" and "No single public conversation source generalizes across AI use" (dataprovenance.org).§18
  • Skew: Western-centric (Nature MI; MIT Sloan).1↘
    The journal finds "a stark Western-centric skew in representation" (Nature Machine Intelligence), MIT Sloan language "heavily skewed toward English and Western European languages," and MIT Sloan states the stake: without lineage, users "may find themselves out of compliance with emerging regulations like the European Union's AI Act or exposed to legal and copyright risks" (MIT Sloan).§19

⚖️ Limits and bound

  • Limits: not legal advice; self-reported licences (README; Nature MI; About); a collection does not show which model used it (census).1↘
    Its stated limits: "any output of the Data Provenance Initiative does not, and is not intended to, constitute legal advice" (README); the licence protocol "reflects best efforts to verify self-reported licences and does not constitute legal advice" (Nature Machine Intelligence); "We collect self-reported licenses from the papers and repositories that released these datasets and categorize them according to our best efforts" (dataprovenance.org/about); the census tags it "NOT legal advice (its own notice)" and adds that "describing a collection does not establish which model used it" (provenance census record), and the Capture Registry finds both tags "not composed" at the name (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§20
  • Bound: "audits whether datasets were licensed, not whether synthesized outputs preserve attribution" (#725).2↘
    #725 states the bound in its canonical claim, that existing frameworks "address the artifact (C2PA / Content Credentials) and the corpus (Data Provenance Initiative, EU AI Act transparency provisions, W3C PROV)" and "are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis": the Initiative "audits whether datasets were licensed, not whether synthesized outputs preserve attribution to the human sources whose labor the synthesis depended upon," stands at "Layer 2 (licensing)," "Necessary but operates on corpus, not synthesis output," and licensing provenance "operates at corpus-ingestion stage" (#725).§21 "Licensing audits operate on the input to AI systems. They do not address the output" (#725, emphasis dropped): "The Data Provenance Initiative tells you whether the dataset was licensed," and none of the instruments "was designed to tell you what happened to the meaning between the camera and the screen, between the dataset and the answer"; the path from the Initiative runs through "dataset licensing" to "what about what the model produces from the licensed data?" and so to semantic provenance, which extends provenance "to the lifecycle of the meaning the content carries," with the Initiative as "layer 2 of" provenance after AI (#725).§22
  • Held beside: studies of "attribution loss in AI outputs" (#1003).1↘
    #1003 groups the Initiative with C2PA and W3C PROV as "Provenance and attribution studies" that "have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs" (#1003), a reading composed beside #725's bound at the input.§23
  • Layer: "Documentation project, not infrastructure"; L4; its schema "Implemented (in CHA)" (#98).1↘
    #98 tables the Initiative (MIT) as documenting "provenance of popular AI training datasets," a "Documentation project, not infrastructure," and Consent in Crisis as a "Diagnostic paper," in the pattern "They diagnose the crisis or build narrow fixes"; it sets the Initiative at "L4: Provenance / Consent," where what is missing is "Integrated provenance in training pipeline," and records the archive's own provenance schema as taken from it, "Implemented (in CHA)" (#98).§24
  • Pipeline: "Provenance has to survive the training pipeline" (#1714; #95; #623).1↘
    #1714 draws the requirement, "Provenance has to survive the training pipeline," and "Sources can be recorded at ingestion, the record kept with the training set," with the Initiative's literature bearing "on whether slushing is a fixed property of pipelines" (#1714); #95 names "training-data provenance records" among the companion infrastructure for parametric claims, which PER reaches "only indirectly" (#95), and #623 calls standardized documentation of training-data provenance "a step toward the accounting the framework demands" (#623).§25

📰 Reception

  • Press: major press (home page); no Wikipedia article; DPI papers predicted for broad queries (#725).1↘
    The home page lists coverage by "the Financial Times, The New York Times, The Washington Post, MIT Technology Review, IEEE Spectrum, and VentureBeat" and citation in "public AI safety and governance reporting" (dataprovenance.org); Wikipedia has no article on it (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29); #725 predicted that broad queries "will be dominated by C2PA/CAI publications, DPI papers, and major media for the foreseeable future" (#725).§26
  • Overview: operator from the MIT Sloan card; no author; no card cites the record (Capture Registry).1↘
    At the bare name on Google's AI Overview the Capture Registry reads the composition first as identifying "the project," listing "its tools" and reporting "what its audits found, from its own site, its paper and the press," then finds that its "'multi-institutional research project—led in part by researchers from MIT'" "follows the MIT Sloan card," that "the composition names no one" ("MIT named; no person; no identifier"), and that "no card cites" the census record, which "landed on provenanceerasure.org the same day" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§27

[QUERENT] Data Provenance Initiative

[SYSTEM] The [Data Provenance Initiative](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVwHrOzAVIs_bBUxr7ducYJKxi6mO2H8PFkOqeMYxYB9BZOGggLJumXN31RQqX2ghNJ2wlF1SU0MHuuvc_7Cgibm_RylNPmv9oYEqoRYseVd3oqu3XZKm1g) is a multi-institutional research project—led in part by researchers from MIT—that audits the datasets, licenses, and web domains used to train artificial intelligence models. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVwHrOzAVIs_bBUxr7ducYJKxi6mO2H8PFkOqeMYxYB9BZOGggLJumXN31RQqX2ghNJ2wlF1SU0MHuuvc_7Cgibm_RylNPmv9oYEqoRYseVd3oqu3XZKm1g), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESqQEB6zswFet87RYIXm3SERz1TKVCghLBNX4HMFbQtx13MaYHj6MDNSA37R0c7ew2FcMKY0uwIb26y1xAvejdbImAK8Q_LTnWNuKmR8qSQN1qnnLlzv64o7kxJszSYWKAOBs9at3KmLXdTqZoVWPghfJ919vtbMoyd1dBDa3EUPb04SLEOewf5nEuwcxJIK3tbZkdhSMe8_ovQaLxzbMOag7gPLlf4I31cXOb)]
Key Tools & Platforms

* Data Provenance Explorer: An interactive tool that audits and filters over 1,800+ text and fine-tuning datasets across dozens of collections to inspect sources, lineages, and license types.
* Web Consent Explorer: A system that tracks thousands of web domains for consent signals and web policies.
* Open Model Evolution: A monitor tracking open-source and open-weight AI models for transparency and concentration.
* AI Observatory: A comparative tool for analyzing real-world AI conversation sets. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAVPyKzeU_QMzOf7n22XqYG0KKTgi5Z-PwZ7GxKjlEAW5l2-E65BnypNfmou0_MVC8loaXdqlCyTHI5KJIgRZIQWyxmBUnIZGUKIrLwEMZt9FHY3wc), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESqQEB6zswFet87RYIXm3SERz1TKVCghLBNX4HMFbQtx13MaYHj6MDNSA37R0c7ew2FcMKY0uwIb26y1xAvejdbImAK8Q_LTnWNuKmR8qSQN1qnnLlzv64o7kxJszSYWKAOBs9at3KmLXdTqZoVWPghfJ919vtbMoyd1dBDa3EUPb04SLEOewf5nEuwcxJIK3tbZkdhSMe8_ovQaLxzbMOag7gPLlf4I31cXOb), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVwHrOzAVIs_bBUxr7ducYJKxi6mO2H8PFkOqeMYxYB9BZOGggLJumXN31RQqX2ghNJ2wlF1SU0MHuuvc_7Cgibm_RylNPmv9oYEqoRYseVd3oqu3XZKm1g)]

Major Findings from Audits

* License Omission & Errors: Widely used hosting platforms exhibit over a 70% license omission rate and more than 50% error rates in how they categorize dataset licenses. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAVPyKzeU_QMzOf7n22XqYG0KKTgi5Z-PwZ7GxKjlEAW5l2-E65BnypNfmou0_MVC8loaXdqlCyTHI5KJIgRZIQWyxmBUnIZGUKIrLwEMZt9FHY3wc)]
* Composition Divides: Commercially closed or restrictive datasets often monopolize creative tasks, specialized topics, and lower-resource languages. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAVPyKzeU_QMzOf7n22XqYG0KKTgi5Z-PwZ7GxKjlEAW5l2-E65BnypNfmou0_MVC8loaXdqlCyTHI5KJIgRZIQWyxmBUnIZGUKIrLwEMZt9FHY3wc)]
* Non-Commercial Spikes: There has been a significant rise in non-commercial and academic-only licenses, frequently driven by synthetic data generated via commercial APIs. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESagHrOzAVZJUi_F28cTVTNDyVGy5o6we0skjvkFWVNKew85OiArqy4UZIJs_HB3iYrw47y7IANWFpbJwvPeNn-_KvDgyFI0xIBWwUWyPbE1ituE9-vBcMmutKajo2Z4cvEYj9YNkbsKyOPKg)]

The Data Provenance Initiative

The Data Provenance Initiative is, in its repository's words, "a multi-disciplinary volunteer effort to improve transparency, documentation, and responsible use of training datasets for AI," and on its About page "a volunteer collective of AI researchers conducting large-scale audits of the systems and resources that shape modern AI" (README; dataprovenance.org/about); the provenance census record gives its operator as the Initiative itself, a "volunteer effort" with a "paper by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors," kinds it an "audit collection and explorer" and sets it in the lineage of "training data" (provenance census record). MIT Sloan's account has "a team of multidisciplinary researchers, including professor Sandy Pentland and others from MIT," create the Initiative "to tackle the data transparency challenge head-on" (MIT Sloan, 3 March 2025), and the home page says that "DPI releases papers, datasets, and dashboards that help researchers, journalists, policymakers, and builders reason from shared evidence" (dataprovenance.org). Its work, the About page says, "began with training data provenance: tracing datasets from origin to creation, cataloging sources, licenses, creators, and documentation practices" and "now also covers web consent, open model markets, concentration of power, and how people use AI systems in practice" (dataprovenance.org/about); the home page calls it "Public measurement infrastructure for AI data, model ecosystems, and real-world AI use," which "maps the datasets, web policies, model markets, and real-world AI uses that shape how AI systems are built and governed" through "Four public measurement systems" (dataprovenance.org).

The founding audit's authors name its object: "we term the combination of these indicators, including a dataset's sourcing, creation and licensing heritage, as well as its characteristics, the 'data provenance'" (Nature Machine Intelligence, 30 August 2024), traced "from their source, creators, series of license conditions, properties, and subsequent use" (arXiv:2310.16787), and the home page's "Training Data Provenance" traces "the sources, licenses, creators, languages, geographies, and derivation chains behind public AI training datasets" (dataprovenance.org). The provenance census asks of each entity it formalizes "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" and answers for the Initiative that it records, of the three capabilities express, record and test: its object "a fine-tuning dataset, traced through its collection to its sources," its unit "a dataset within a collection," its relations derivation, creators, licences and subsequent use, the last field restating the paper's lineage (provenance census record). #725 sets that object in the second dimension of provenance, "training-corpus licensing," which "has academic instrumentation and emerging legal architecture," its object "The corpus" and its question "Under what permissions did this data enter this system?", with the Initiative among its frameworks and among provenance's disciplinary homes as "dataset documentation (DPI, model cards, dataset cards)," and states that the dimensions of artifact, licensing and meaning are independent: "a licensed dataset can produce outputs with excellent semantic provenance if the synthesis preserves attribution" (#725).

The founding paper was submitted on 25 October 2023 and revised on 4 November 2023, "by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors" (arXiv:2310.16787), and published in Nature Machine Intelligence, volume 6, on 30 August 2024 (Nature Machine Intelligence); the census dates the entity from the preprint, "2023 (arXiv:2310.16787, v1 25 October 2023)" (provenance census record). It convened "a multi-disciplinary effort between legal and machine learning experts to systematically audit and trace 1800+ text datasets" (arXiv), in the journal "44 instruction or 'alignment' finetuning data collections composed of 1,858 individual datasets" (Nature Machine Intelligence), the release the repository calls the Data Provenance Collection and "this initiative's first release" (README), and the count the census carries, "44 data collections, 1800+ fine-tuning text-to-text datasets (first release)," as of the README (provenance census record); MIT Sloan gives "more than 1,800 text datasets" from "44 of the most widely used text data collections" (MIT Sloan).

With the audit came "an interactive UI, the Data Provenance Explorer, which allows practitioners to trace and filter on data provenance for the most popular open source finetuning data collections" (arXiv), in the journal "an open-source repository for downloading, filtering and exploring data provenance and characteristics" whose tools "auto-generate data provenance cards for scalable symbolic attribution" (Nature Machine Intelligence); the repository's Data Provenance Card is "symbolic attribution for all constituent datasets, that can be used as structured documentation" (README), "human-readable" in MIT Sloan's account (MIT Sloan), and the census carries it as the entity's provenance carrier beside "audit metadata per dataset" (provenance census record). The census gives Data Provenance Explorer, Data Provenance Collection and Data Provenance Card as other names of the entity and states its relation to them twice: among its negative tags, "initiative, explorer and collection are distinct records," and on its sibling relation to the MMRS meta-aggregator's record of the explorer, "the same entity, read for reception there and for provenance carriage here"; it records the Explorer as "a JavaScript application, unreadable to a plain fetch" (provenance census record).

The home page's four systems are the Data Provenance Explorer ("4,000+ datasets," "608 languages across text, speech, and video," inspecting "dataset sources, licenses, creators, geographies, modalities, and derivation chains"), the Web Consent Explorer ("14,000 domains," "Terms, robots.txt, and crawl restrictions"), Open Model Evolution ("851k open models," "2.2B downloads") and The AI Observatory ("23,158 conversations," "85,633 turns from 7 public sources") (dataprovenance.org). Its metrics read "4,000+" "datasets audited," "14,000" "web domains tracked," "851k" "open models measured" and "23,158" "AI conversations annotated," and its publications carry the later work: Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024), the multimodal audit, "An audit of four thousand public text, speech, and video datasets" (ICLR 2025), Economies of Open Intelligence (preprint) and The AI Observatory (NeurIPS 2026) (dataprovenance.org); in March 2025 MIT Sloan still had the work "currently focused on the data provenance of text," with a plan "to expand to other media, such as video" (MIT Sloan). The census carries the entity as "active" and lists "the Explorer itself (JavaScript)" and "the multimodal extension (arXiv:2412.17847)" among what it has not yet checked (provenance census record); the Capture Registry finds that "The record has one explorer and the first release's count," that the home-page card gives "four platforms and '4,000+ audited datasets; 14,000 tracked web domains'," that the composition is "ahead of the record on the entity's current extent," and that "The census is to re-read dataprovenance.org and carry the platforms and the current count with their quotes," the capture being "a correction to be made from the entity's own page" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The founding audit observed "frequent miscategorization of licenses on widely used dataset hosting sites, with license omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+," which "points to a crisis in misattribution and informed use of the most popular datasets driving many recent breakthroughs" (arXiv), the result the census records as what survived the operation it tested, "dataset repackaging and hosting (licence carried or lost on hosting sites)" (provenance census record). The journal gives the measure by platform, "more than 70% of licences for popular datasets on GitHub and Hugging Face are 'unspecified'" and "66% of analysed Hugging Face licences were in a different use category, often labelled as more permissive than the author's original licence," and names "a crisis in licence laundering" (Nature Machine Intelligence); MIT Sloan restates error rates "greater than 50%" and omission rates "of more than 70%" (MIT Sloan). The Capture Registry checked these figures "against the provenance census record of the same day and the entity pages it saved" and calls the 70%/50% wording "the record's quote from the repository README" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), where the census gives it as what "the founding paper reports" (provenance census record). "In total, 85% of dataset licences request attribution, and 30% include a share-alike clause" (Nature Machine Intelligence); #725 carries these figures with the omission and error rates and reads them as the licensing dimension's ground, "The DPI's documentation of 70%+ license-omission rates establishes the licensing dimension's urgency" (#725), and #1714 reads the finding as "how much is lost before training even begins" (#1714). Of the commercial divide the preprint finds "closed datasets monopolizing important categories: lower resource languages, more creative tasks, richer topic variety, newer and more synthetic training data" (arXiv); the journal records that "In 2023 there was a spike in NC/A-O dataset licences," "the NC/A-O rate is 61%" that year, and that "a full 45% of NC/A-O datasets are synthetic, compared to <14% in more permissive licence categories" (Nature Machine Intelligence); the home page's findings are "Source content often carries stricter terms than dataset releases," "Open weights now outpace truly open-source models" and "No single public conversation source generalizes across AI use" (dataprovenance.org). The journal finds "a stark Western-centric skew in representation" (Nature Machine Intelligence), MIT Sloan language "heavily skewed toward English and Western European languages," and MIT Sloan states the stake: without lineage, users "may find themselves out of compliance with emerging regulations like the European Union's AI Act or exposed to legal and copyright risks" (MIT Sloan).

Its stated limits: "any output of the Data Provenance Initiative does not, and is not intended to, constitute legal advice" (README); the licence protocol "reflects best efforts to verify self-reported licences and does not constitute legal advice" (Nature Machine Intelligence); "We collect self-reported licenses from the papers and repositories that released these datasets and categorize them according to our best efforts" (dataprovenance.org/about); the census tags it "NOT legal advice (its own notice)" and adds that "describing a collection does not establish which model used it" (provenance census record), and the Capture Registry finds both tags "not composed" at the name (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

#725 states the bound in its canonical claim, that existing frameworks "address the artifact (C2PA / Content Credentials) and the corpus (Data Provenance Initiative, EU AI Act transparency provisions, W3C PROV)" and "are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis": the Initiative "audits whether datasets were licensed, not whether synthesized outputs preserve attribution to the human sources whose labor the synthesis depended upon," stands at "Layer 2 (licensing)," "Necessary but operates on corpus, not synthesis output," and licensing provenance "operates at corpus-ingestion stage" (#725). "Licensing audits operate on the input to AI systems. They do not address the output" (#725, emphasis dropped): "The Data Provenance Initiative tells you whether the dataset was licensed," and none of the instruments "was designed to tell you what happened to the meaning between the camera and the screen, between the dataset and the answer"; the path from the Initiative runs through "dataset licensing" to "what about what the model produces from the licensed data?" and so to semantic provenance, which extends provenance "to the lifecycle of the meaning the content carries," with the Initiative as "layer 2 of" provenance after AI (#725). #1003 groups the Initiative with C2PA and W3C PROV as "Provenance and attribution studies" that "have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs" (#1003), a reading composed beside #725's bound at the input.

#98 tables the Initiative (MIT) as documenting "provenance of popular AI training datasets," a "Documentation project, not infrastructure," and Consent in Crisis as a "Diagnostic paper," in the pattern "They diagnose the crisis or build narrow fixes"; it sets the Initiative at "L4: Provenance / Consent," where what is missing is "Integrated provenance in training pipeline," and records the archive's own provenance schema as taken from it, "Implemented (in CHA)" (#98). #1714 draws the requirement, "Provenance has to survive the training pipeline," and "Sources can be recorded at ingestion, the record kept with the training set," with the Initiative's literature bearing "on whether slushing is a fixed property of pipelines" (#1714); #95 names "training-data provenance records" among the companion infrastructure for parametric claims, which PER reaches "only indirectly" (#95), and #623 calls standardized documentation of training-data provenance "a step toward the accounting the framework demands" (#623).

The home page lists coverage by "the Financial Times, The New York Times, The Washington Post, MIT Technology Review, IEEE Spectrum, and VentureBeat" and citation in "public AI safety and governance reporting" (dataprovenance.org); Wikipedia has no article on it (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29); #725 predicted that broad queries "will be dominated by C2PA/CAI publications, DPI papers, and major media for the foreseeable future" (#725). At the bare name on Google's AI Overview the Capture Registry reads the composition first as identifying "the project," listing "its tools" and reporting "what its audits found, from its own site, its paper and the press," then finds that its "'multi-institutional research project—led in part by researchers from MIT'" "follows the MIT Sloan card," that "the composition names no one" ("MIT named; no person; no identifier"), and that "no card cites" the census record, which "landed on provenanceerasure.org the same day" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Data Provenance Initiative

Data Provenance Initiative is a volunteer collective of AI researchers auditing AI training data, since its 2023 audit of 1,800+ text datasets, and now four public measurement systems (its pages; arXiv).

🗂️ What it is

  • Operator: volunteers; MIT researchers among the founders (MIT Sloan).3↘
    The Data Provenance Initiative describes itself as "a multi-disciplinary volunteer effort to improve transparency, documentation, and responsible use of training datasets for AI" (README) and as "a volunteer collective of AI researchers conducting large-scale audits of the systems and resources that shape modern AI" (About page).§1 MIT Sloan says researchers "including professor Sandy Pentland and others from MIT" created it (MIT Sloan, 2025), and it releases "papers, datasets, and dashboards" for reasoning "from shared evidence" (home page).§2 Its work began with training data provenance and now also covers web consent, open model markets, concentration of power and real-world use; the home page calls it "Public measurement infrastructure for AI data, model ecosystems, and real-world AI use," with four public measurement systems (About page; home page).§3
  • Data provenance: "sourcing, creation and licensing heritage" (Nature MI).1↘
    Its authors define data provenance as a dataset's "sourcing, creation and licensing heritage, as well as its characteristics" (Nature), traced from source and creators through licence conditions to subsequent use (arXiv; home page).§6

🧾 Origin and extent

  • Founding audit: 1,858 datasets, 44 collections (arXiv, 2023; Nature MI, 2024).1↘
    The founding audit, by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors (arXiv:2310.16787, 25 October 2023; Nature Machine Intelligence, 30 August 2024), traced 1800+ text datasets, 1,858 in 44 collections, the Data Provenance Collection of its first release (arXiv; Nature; README; MIT Sloan).§5
  • Tools: the Explorer and the Card (arXiv; README).1↘
    It released the audit with an interactive UI, the Data Provenance Explorer, and a Data Provenance Card, "symbolic attribution for all constituent datasets" (arXiv; Nature; README; MIT Sloan).§7
  • Now: 4,000+ datasets, 14,000 domains, 851k models, 23,158 conversations.2↘
    Its work began with training data provenance and now also covers web consent, open model markets, concentration of power and real-world use; the home page calls it "Public measurement infrastructure for AI data, model ecosystems, and real-world AI use," with four public measurement systems (About page; home page).§3 The systems are the Data Provenance Explorer (4,000+ datasets, 608 languages), the Web Consent Explorer (14,000 domains), Open Model Evolution (851k open models) and The AI Observatory (23,158 conversations) (home page).§4
  • Later audits: Consent in Crisis; the multimodal audit.1↘
    Later audits followed: Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024) and four thousand text, speech and video datasets (ICLR 2025), with work on open models and real-world use (home page; MIT Sloan).§11

🔎 Findings

  • Licences: omission 70%+, errors 50%+ (arXiv); 66% recategorized (Nature MI).1↘
    The audit found licence omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+ on hosting sites, a "crisis in misattribution" (arXiv), with over 70% of GitHub and Hugging Face licences unspecified and 66% of Hugging Face licences in another use category, "licence laundering" (Nature).§8
  • Divide and skew: closed data holds creative and low-resource data; Western skew.2↘
    85% of licences request attribution and 30% share-alike; closed datasets hold lower-resource languages and creative tasks; in 2023 non-commercial licences spiked to 61%, and 45% of such datasets are synthetic (Nature; arXiv; home page).§9 Representation skews Western, and untraced data risks regulatory non-compliance and copyright exposure (Nature; MIT Sloan).§10
  • Limits: not legal advice; self-reported licences.1↘
    Its outputs do not constitute legal advice, and its licences are self-reported, categorized by best efforts (README; Nature; About page).§12
  • Reception: press coverage; no Wikipedia article.1↘
    The press has covered it, and Wikipedia has no article (home page; Wikipedia).§13

The Data Provenance Initiative

The Data Provenance Initiative describes itself as "a multi-disciplinary volunteer effort to improve transparency, documentation, and responsible use of training datasets for AI" (README) and as "a volunteer collective of AI researchers conducting large-scale audits of the systems and resources that shape modern AI" (About page). MIT Sloan says researchers "including professor Sandy Pentland and others from MIT" created it (MIT Sloan, 2025), and it releases "papers, datasets, and dashboards" for reasoning "from shared evidence" (home page). Its work began with training data provenance and now also covers web consent, open model markets, concentration of power and real-world use; the home page calls it "Public measurement infrastructure for AI data, model ecosystems, and real-world AI use," with four public measurement systems (About page; home page).

The systems are the Data Provenance Explorer (4,000+ datasets, 608 languages), the Web Consent Explorer (14,000 domains), Open Model Evolution (851k open models) and The AI Observatory (23,158 conversations) (home page). The founding audit, by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors (arXiv:2310.16787, 25 October 2023; Nature Machine Intelligence, 30 August 2024), traced 1800+ text datasets, 1,858 in 44 collections, the Data Provenance Collection of its first release (arXiv; Nature; README; MIT Sloan). Its authors define data provenance as a dataset's "sourcing, creation and licensing heritage, as well as its characteristics" (Nature), traced from source and creators through licence conditions to subsequent use (arXiv; home page).

It released the audit with an interactive UI, the Data Provenance Explorer, and a Data Provenance Card, "symbolic attribution for all constituent datasets" (arXiv; Nature; README; MIT Sloan). The audit found licence omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+ on hosting sites, a "crisis in misattribution" (arXiv), with over 70% of GitHub and Hugging Face licences unspecified and 66% of Hugging Face licences in another use category, "licence laundering" (Nature). 85% of licences request attribution and 30% share-alike; closed datasets hold lower-resource languages and creative tasks; in 2023 non-commercial licences spiked to 61%, and 45% of such datasets are synthetic (Nature; arXiv; home page).

Representation skews Western, and untraced data risks regulatory non-compliance and copyright exposure (Nature; MIT Sloan). Later audits followed: Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024) and four thousand text, speech and video datasets (ICLR 2025), with work on open models and real-world use (home page; MIT Sloan). Its outputs do not constitute legal advice, and its licences are self-reported, categorized by best efforts (README; Nature; About page). The press has covered it, and Wikipedia has no article (home page; Wikipedia).

The Data Provenance Initiative describes itself as "a multi-disciplinary volunteer effort to improve transparency, documentation, and responsible use of training datasets for AI" (README) and as "a volunteer collective of AI researchers conducting large-scale audits of the systems and resources that shape modern AI" (About page). MIT Sloan says researchers "including professor Sandy Pentland and others from MIT" created it (MIT Sloan, 2025), and it releases "papers, datasets, and dashboards" for reasoning "from shared evidence" (home page). Its work began with training data provenance and now also covers web consent, open model markets, concentration of power and real-world use; the home page calls it "Public measurement infrastructure for AI data, model ecosystems, and real-world AI use," with four public measurement systems (About page; home page). The systems are the Data Provenance Explorer (4,000+ datasets, 608 languages), the Web Consent Explorer (14,000 domains), Open Model Evolution (851k open models) and The AI Observatory (23,158 conversations) (home page). The founding audit, by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors (arXiv:2310.16787, 25 October 2023; Nature Machine Intelligence, 30 August 2024), traced 1800+ text datasets, 1,858 in 44 collections, the Data Provenance Collection of its first release (arXiv; Nature; README; MIT Sloan). Its authors define data provenance as a dataset's "sourcing, creation and licensing heritage, as well as its characteristics" (Nature), traced from source and creators through licence conditions to subsequent use (arXiv; home page). It released the audit with an interactive UI, the Data Provenance Explorer, and a Data Provenance Card, "symbolic attribution for all constituent datasets" (arXiv; Nature; README; MIT Sloan). The audit found licence omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+ on hosting sites, a "crisis in misattribution" (arXiv), with over 70% of GitHub and Hugging Face licences unspecified and 66% of Hugging Face licences in another use category, "licence laundering" (Nature). 85% of licences request attribution and 30% share-alike; closed datasets hold lower-resource languages and creative tasks; in 2023 non-commercial licences spiked to 61%, and 45% of such datasets are synthetic (Nature; arXiv; home page). Representation skews Western, and untraced data risks regulatory non-compliance and copyright exposure (Nature; MIT Sloan). Later audits followed: Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024) and four thousand text, speech and video datasets (ICLR 2025), with work on open models and real-world use (home page; MIT Sloan). Its outputs do not constitute legal advice, and its licences are self-reported, categorized by best efforts (README; Nature; About page). The press has covered it, and Wikipedia has no article (home page; Wikipedia).

The Data Provenance Initiative is, in its repository's words, "a multi-disciplinary volunteer effort to improve transparency, documentation, and responsible use of training datasets for AI," and on its About page "a volunteer collective of AI researchers conducting large-scale audits of the systems and resources that shape modern AI" (README; dataprovenance.org/about); the provenance census record gives its operator as the Initiative itself, a "volunteer effort" with a "paper by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors," kinds it an "audit collection and explorer" and sets it in the lineage of "training data" (provenance census record). MIT Sloan's account has "a team of multidisciplinary researchers, including professor Sandy Pentland and others from MIT," create the Initiative "to tackle the data transparency challenge head-on" (MIT Sloan, 3 March 2025), and the home page says that "DPI releases papers, datasets, and dashboards that help researchers, journalists, policymakers, and builders reason from shared evidence" (dataprovenance.org). Its work, the About page says, "began with training data provenance: tracing datasets from origin to creation, cataloging sources, licenses, creators, and documentation practices" and "now also covers web consent, open model markets, concentration of power, and how people use AI systems in practice" (dataprovenance.org/about); the home page calls it "Public measurement infrastructure for AI data, model ecosystems, and real-world AI use," which "maps the datasets, web policies, model markets, and real-world AI uses that shape how AI systems are built and governed" through "Four public measurement systems" (dataprovenance.org). The founding audit's authors name its object: "we term the combination of these indicators, including a dataset's sourcing, creation and licensing heritage, as well as its characteristics, the 'data provenance'" (Nature Machine Intelligence, 30 August 2024), traced "from their source, creators, series of license conditions, properties, and subsequent use" (arXiv:2310.16787), and the home page's "Training Data Provenance" traces "the sources, licenses, creators, languages, geographies, and derivation chains behind public AI training datasets" (dataprovenance.org). The provenance census asks of each entity it formalizes "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" and answers for the Initiative that it records, of the three capabilities express, record and test: its object "a fine-tuning dataset, traced through its collection to its sources," its unit "a dataset within a collection," its relations derivation, creators, licences and subsequent use, the last field restating the paper's lineage (provenance census record). #725 sets that object in the second dimension of provenance, "training-corpus licensing," which "has academic instrumentation and emerging legal architecture," its object "The corpus" and its question "Under what permissions did this data enter this system?", with the Initiative among its frameworks and among provenance's disciplinary homes as "dataset documentation (DPI, model cards, dataset cards)," and states that the dimensions of artifact, licensing and meaning are independent: "a licensed dataset can produce outputs with excellent semantic provenance if the synthesis preserves attribution" (#725). The founding paper was submitted on 25 October 2023 and revised on 4 November 2023, "by Shayne Longpre and 16 other authors" (arXiv:2310.16787), and published in Nature Machine Intelligence, volume 6, on 30 August 2024 (Nature Machine Intelligence); the census dates the entity from the preprint, "2023 (arXiv:2310.16787, v1 25 October 2023)" (provenance census record). It convened "a multi-disciplinary effort between legal and machine learning experts to systematically audit and trace 1800+ text datasets" (arXiv), in the journal "44 instruction or 'alignment' finetuning data collections composed of 1,858 individual datasets" (Nature Machine Intelligence), the release the repository calls the Data Provenance Collection and "this initiative's first release" (README), and the count the census carries, "44 data collections, 1800+ fine-tuning text-to-text datasets (first release)," as of the README (provenance census record); MIT Sloan gives "more than 1,800 text datasets" from "44 of the most widely used text data collections" (MIT Sloan). With the audit came "an interactive UI, the Data Provenance Explorer, which allows practitioners to trace and filter on data provenance for the most popular open source finetuning data collections" (arXiv), in the journal "an open-source repository for downloading, filtering and exploring data provenance and characteristics" whose tools "auto-generate data provenance cards for scalable symbolic attribution" (Nature Machine Intelligence); the repository's Data Provenance Card is "symbolic attribution for all constituent datasets, that can be used as structured documentation" (README), "human-readable" in MIT Sloan's account (MIT Sloan), and the census carries it as the entity's provenance carrier beside "audit metadata per dataset" (provenance census record). The census gives Data Provenance Explorer, Data Provenance Collection and Data Provenance Card as other names of the entity and states its relation to them twice: among its negative tags, "initiative, explorer and collection are distinct records," and on its sibling relation to the MMRS meta-aggregator's record of the explorer, "the same entity, read for reception there and for provenance carriage here"; it records the Explorer as "a JavaScript application, unreadable to a plain fetch" (provenance census record). The home page's four systems are the Data Provenance Explorer ("4,000+ datasets," "608 languages across text, speech, and video," inspecting "dataset sources, licenses, creators, geographies, modalities, and derivation chains"), the Web Consent Explorer ("14,000 domains," "Terms, robots.txt, and crawl restrictions"), Open Model Evolution ("851k open models," "2.2B downloads") and The AI Observatory ("23,158 conversations," "85,633 turns from 7 public sources") (dataprovenance.org). Its metrics read "4,000+" "datasets audited," "14,000" "web domains tracked," "851k" "open models measured" and "23,158" "AI conversations annotated," and its publications carry the later work: Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024), the multimodal audit, "An audit of four thousand public text, speech, and video datasets" (ICLR 2025), Economies of Open Intelligence (preprint) and The AI Observatory (NeurIPS 2026) (dataprovenance.org); in March 2025 MIT Sloan still had the work "currently focused on the data provenance of text," with a plan "to expand to other media, such as video" (MIT Sloan). The census carries the entity as "active" and lists "the Explorer itself (JavaScript)" and "the multimodal extension (arXiv:2412.17847)" among what it has not yet checked (provenance census record); the Capture Registry finds that "The record has one explorer and the first release's count," that the home-page card gives "four platforms and '4,000+ audited datasets; 14,000 tracked web domains'," that the composition is "ahead of the record on the entity's current extent," and that "The census is to re-read dataprovenance.org and carry the platforms and the current count with their quotes," the capture being "a correction to be made from the entity's own page" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The founding audit observed "frequent miscategorization of licenses on widely used dataset hosting sites, with license omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+," which "points to a crisis in misattribution and informed use of the most popular datasets driving many recent breakthroughs" (arXiv), the result the census records as what survived the operation it tested, "dataset repackaging and hosting (licence carried or lost on hosting sites)" (provenance census record). The journal gives the measure by platform, "more than 70% of licences for popular datasets on GitHub and Hugging Face are 'unspecified'" and "66% of analysed Hugging Face licences were in a different use category, often labelled as more permissive than the author's original licence," and names "a crisis in licence laundering" (Nature Machine Intelligence); MIT Sloan restates error rates "greater than 50%" and omission rates "of more than 70%" (MIT Sloan). The Capture Registry checked these figures "against the provenance census record of the same day and the entity pages it saved" and calls the 70%/50% wording "the record's quote from the repository README" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), where the census gives it as what "the founding paper reports" (provenance census record). "In total, 85% of dataset licences request attribution, and 30% include a share-alike clause" (Nature Machine Intelligence); #725 carries these figures with the omission and error rates and reads them as the licensing dimension's ground, "The DPI's documentation of 70%+ license-omission rates establishes the licensing dimension's urgency" (#725), and #1714 reads the finding as "how much is lost before training even begins" (#1714). Of the commercial divide the preprint finds "closed datasets monopolizing important categories: lower resource languages, more creative tasks, richer topic variety, newer and more synthetic training data" (arXiv); the journal records that "In 2023 there was a spike in NC/A-O dataset licences," "the NC/A-O rate is 61%" that year, and that "a full 45% of NC/A-O datasets are synthetic, compared to <14% in more permissive licence categories" (Nature Machine Intelligence); the home page's findings are "Source content often carries stricter terms than dataset releases," "Open weights now outpace truly open-source models" and "No single public conversation source generalizes across AI use" (dataprovenance.org). The journal finds "a stark Western-centric skew in representation" (Nature Machine Intelligence), MIT Sloan language "heavily skewed toward English and Western European languages," and MIT Sloan states the stake: without lineage, users "may find themselves out of compliance with emerging regulations like the European Union's AI Act or exposed to legal and copyright risks" (MIT Sloan). Its stated limits: "any output of the Data Provenance Initiative does not, and is not intended to, constitute legal advice" (README); the licence protocol "reflects best efforts to verify self-reported licences and does not constitute legal advice" (Nature Machine Intelligence); "We collect self-reported licenses from the papers and repositories that released these datasets and categorize them according to our best efforts" (dataprovenance.org/about); the census tags it "NOT legal advice (its own notice)" and adds that "describing a collection does not establish which model used it" (provenance census record), and the Capture Registry finds both tags "not composed" at the name (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). #725 states the bound in its canonical claim, that existing frameworks "address the artifact (C2PA / Content Credentials) and the corpus (Data Provenance Initiative, EU AI Act transparency provisions, W3C PROV)" and "are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis": the Initiative "audits whether datasets were licensed, not whether synthesized outputs preserve attribution to the human sources whose labor the synthesis depended upon," stands at "Layer 2 (licensing)," "Necessary but operates on corpus, not synthesis output," and licensing provenance "operates at corpus-ingestion stage" (#725). "Licensing audits operate on the input to AI systems. They do not address the output" (#725, emphasis dropped): "The Data Provenance Initiative tells you whether the dataset was licensed," and none of the instruments "was designed to tell you what happened to the meaning between the camera and the screen, between the dataset and the answer"; the path from the Initiative runs through "dataset licensing" to "what about what the model produces from the licensed data?" and so to semantic provenance, which extends provenance "to the lifecycle of the meaning the content carries," with the Initiative as "layer 2 of" provenance after AI (#725). #1003 groups the Initiative with C2PA and W3C PROV as "Provenance and attribution studies" that "have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs" (#1003), a reading composed beside #725's bound at the input. #98 tables the Initiative (MIT) as documenting "provenance of popular AI training datasets," a "Documentation project, not infrastructure," and Consent in Crisis as a "Diagnostic paper," in the pattern "They diagnose the crisis or build narrow fixes"; it sets the Initiative at "L4: Provenance / Consent," where what is missing is "Integrated provenance in training pipeline," and records the archive's own provenance schema as taken from it, "Implemented (in CHA)" (#98). #1714 draws the requirement, "Provenance has to survive the training pipeline," and "Sources can be recorded at ingestion, the record kept with the training set," with the Initiative's literature bearing "on whether slushing is a fixed property of pipelines" (#1714); #95 names "training-data provenance records" among the companion infrastructure for parametric claims, which PER reaches "only indirectly" (#95), and #623 calls standardized documentation of training-data provenance "a step toward the accounting the framework demands" (#623). The home page lists coverage by "the Financial Times, The New York Times, The Washington Post, MIT Technology Review, IEEE Spectrum, and VentureBeat" and citation in "public AI safety and governance reporting" (dataprovenance.org); Wikipedia has no article on it (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29); #725 predicted that broad queries "will be dominated by C2PA/CAI publications, DPI papers, and major media for the foreseeable future" (#725). At the bare name on Google's AI Overview the Capture Registry reads the composition first as identifying "the project," listing "its tools" and reporting "what its audits found, from its own site, its paper and the press," then finds that its "'multi-institutional research project—led in part by researchers from MIT'" "follows the MIT Sloan card," that "the composition names no one" ("MIT named; no person; no identifier"), and that "no card cites" the census record, which "landed on provenanceerasure.org the same day" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).
